This design doc is used to align on a high-level plan for the reimplementation of the QTD3 app functionality.

## Background

- QTD1 (see [`qtd1.qmd`](qtd1.qmd)) was limited to fixed designs (without interim analysis) and non-Bayesian decision rules. 
- Developed 2-3 years later, QTD2 and then later QTD3 represent an entirely different application, allowing for Bayesian interim analyses and utilizing double-criterion decision rules. The approach is described in @gsponer2014.
- The code for continuous endpoints is based on the `gsbDesign` R package [@gerber2024] (which itself partially uses the `gsDesign` R package), which is described by @gerber2016.
    - The `gsbDesign` R package was written by Florian Gerber, who was an intern at that time. Björn took over maintenance on CRAN, but he doesn't think it fulfills standard quality criterias in terms of software development. 
    - After looking at the package, Daniel confirmed that we need a reimplementation of `gsbDesign`
- For binary endpoints the internally developed R package `BinaryTrial` is used. This was never released on CRAN and is quite old (but already in R package format).
    - See `QTD_material\QTD3\BinaryTrial` for the source package
    - This was written by Jouni Kerman (now at Google)
    - Björn mentioned he would not recommend building on `BinaryTrial` either
- The GUI code is in Java
    - The binary to execute is `QTD_material\QTD3\QTD-3.0.0\bin\R with QTD3.exe`
    - In order to run this successfully, you have to install the old 32-bit Java SDK and JRE on Windows, see [here](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/jdk-v5-microsoft-windows.html)
    - We also have the Java source code available in `QTD_material\QTD3\java-src\org\gsbgui`, and should be able to find most calls to R from the Java code by recursive file search for `".eval"`
- Internal IT does not like that it is a Desktop application; they have, e.g., security concerns; therefore, they recommend a reimplementation
    - Ideally they would like to have replacements in place by end of 2025
- Additionally, it would be important to have meta-analytic-predictive (MAP) mixture priors included in the new implementation.
    - Standard in Novartis and also used by many other companies
    - One option there would be to use `RBeST` in the backend
- Alexander Przybylski and Dominic Magirr have taken the lead on the QTD replacement project
    - Received feedback that replacement of QTD3 may be of higher priority than QTD1

## `BinaryTrial` review

The `BinaryTrial` package analyses outcomes and operating characteristics for binary trials.
The probabilities of operating characteristics are exact, as each possible outcome is enumerated; no
simulation error is involved.

The main functions in this package are:

- `BinaryTrialDesign()`: Creates an object representing a binary trial design, involving two arms and one or more analyses.
    - contains a function to compute tail probabilities for all possible outcomes in all interim and final analyses
    - returns an object of class `Binary2ArmDesign`, which for the user appears as a data frame with the design parameters for each interim and final look
- `BinaryTrialOC()`: Computes operating characteristics (OC) for the binary trial design. 
    - takes the `Binary2ArmDesign` as input, as well as different scenario specifications.
    - Internally calls the workhorse `.BinaryTrialOC()` function, which does the actual calculations.
        - in turn this calls `postbetatail()` which calls a C function itself
        - Still most of the code is in R
    - returns a data frame with the parameters, and the probabilities of occurrence of each of the decisions computed by the rule
- `BinaryTrialAnalysis()`: returns a data frame of the GO/NOGO/STOP decisions and the underlying
beta difference tail probabilities for all possible outcomes

Notes: 

- Here beta priors are used throughout. So it does not allow for beta mixture priors, which would be needed in the reimplementation.
- Tests are included in the package, which would be helpful for integration tests of a reimplementation later.

## `gsbDesign` review

- Uses a normal approximation for the likelihood, in combination with a normal prior, to achieve normal posteriors
    - Then can either use simulations for OC or numerical integration
- Methods paper already includes example with MAP prior for the control to include historical control information 
    - boiled down to a normal approximation of the control prior though
- For binary outcome, proposes
    - logit transformation to obtain approximate normal logit outcomes
    - for single arm trial use a virtual control arm with precise information in the prior about the assumed control response rate
- For numerical integration, leverages `gsDesign`
    - Translation of posterior distribution critera to observed treatment effect criteria
    - Canonical joint distribution of time point wise treatment effect estimates
    - Bounds are then plugged into `gsProbability()` function to compute the probabilities of the decision rules
    - But it does not work / is not supported when having informative priors on both treatment and control arms

Three main functions needed for the computation of the operating characteristics:

- `gsbDesign()`: fully specifies the design, returns an object of class `gsbDesign`.
- `gsbSimulation()`: specifies the methods for computing the operating characteristics, i.e., whether to use simulation or numerical integration, whether to update per arm or on the treatment effect. The function returns an object of class `gsbSimulation`.
- `gsb()`: calculates the operating characteristics and takes as arguments an object of class `gsbDesign` and an object of class `gsbSimulation`. The function returns an object of class `gsbMainOut`. There are `summary()` and `print()` methods then available for this.

The package source is visible in the read-only CRAN mirror [here](https://github.com/cran/gsbDesign).
Major problems here are that: 

- there is only a single R script file (`package.r`) with almost 3000 lines of code
- there are no tests at all
- internal functions in the file are also not documented, and only `Rd` files are available for the exported functions

## Options for package reimplementation

Here we brainstorm about possible options for reimplementing the QTD3 functionality. These assume that we will not use the existing code in `BinaryTrial` and `gsbDesign` going forward, but can use these for integration tests of the new implementation.

### Option A: `gsbDesign2` comprising continuous and binary endpoints

The idea would be to create a new package `gsbDesign2` which comprises the previous functionality of `gsbDesign`, but also `BinaryTrial`, i.e. exact operating characteristics for binary endpoints.

- The package would be a complete reimplementation of the functionality in `gsbDesign` and `BinaryTrial`, but with a clean code base, state-of-the-art software architecture, proper tests, and documentation.
- The package could use internally `rpact` for the numerical integration for continuous outcomes where possible, which in turn would make validation easier.

### Option B: `rpact.bayes` 

The idea would be to create a new package `rpact.bayes` which would be a Bayesian extension of `rpact`, and a new member in the `rpact` packages family.

- Also here we need to cover in the first place the functionality of `gsbDesign` and `BinaryTrial`, but with a tighter coupling to the `rpact` package
- We would keep the same function name patterns as in the basic `rpact` package to have a consistent and simple user interface
- In a similar way as for `rpact` we would provide formal validation documentation

## Options for GUI reimplementation

Here we brainstorm about possible options for reimplementing the QTD3 GUI. The goal is to have a web-based application that can be used by Novartis employees and external users.

### Option A: Standalone Shiny app reproducing QTD3 app

This could be a new, standalone Shiny app R package, which would be a reimplementation of the QTD3 app.

- The app would be a complete reimplementation of the functionality in QTD3, but with a clean code base, state-of-the-art software architecture, proper tests, and documentation.
- In the backend the GUI uses `rpact.bayes` or `gsbDesign2` for the computations

### Option B: New `rpact.bayes` module in RPACT Cloud

Assuming `rpact.bayes` is the new package for Bayesian designs, we could create a new module in RPACT Cloud which would be a reimplementation of the QTD3 app.

- Code would not be public, but free usage up to certain usage limit for the public
- The app would be hosted on the RPACT Cloud, see [here](https://cloud.rpact.com)
- Installation as part of RPACT Cloud in Novartis internally, easily available in the existing RPACT Cloud deployment; deployment instructions and source code would be available in the Novartis-specific GitHub repository, see [here](https://github.com/rpact-com/rpact.cloud.novartis)
- Other companies licensing RPACT Cloud can also use the app then internally in their own RPACT Cloud

## Options for MAP prior extension

The extension for MAP priors would first need to be explored from a methodology point of view, with appropriate prototype code development. In particular, we would need to understand:

- Can we still use numerical integration via GSD techniques when MAP mixture priors are used?
- If not, can we use more tailored numerical integration?
- If not, do we need MCMC? Then how do we achieve acceptable simulation run times?

## Estimated effort

Here we give a rough estimate of the effort needed for the work packages above. Note that these are rough estimates and may decrease or increase once we have a better understanding of the requirements. The work could be done by RCONIS, Novartis colleagues or in collaboration. 

- Package reimplementation: about 5 months
  - Prototype development: 30 days
  - Translation to C++ (as needed to speed up): 20 days
  - Package development: 20 days
  - Vignettes and examples: 5 days
  - Integration tests vs. existing code: 5 days
  - Validation documentation: 10 days
  - Release on CRAN: 10 days
- GUI reimplementation: about 3 months
  - Prototype development: 20 days
  - Package development: 20 days
  - Integration tests vs. existing app: 5 days
  - Validation documentation: 10 days
  - Release on GitHub: 10 days
- MAP prior extension: about 2.5 months
  - Methodology review and specification: 5 days
  - Prototype development: 15 days
  - Package inclusion: 10 days
  - GUI inclusion: 10 days
  - Update validation documentation: 5 days
  - Release on GitHub: 5 days

  We expect that both Daniel and Friedrich would work on this together as a team, which would reduce the timeline. In particular, we would be able to achieve a reimplementation of the QTD3 app before end of 2025 (and leaving the MAP prior extension to parallel exploration and inclusion in 2026).
